utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, as always, I remind you that you are bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to give the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will begin, as usual, with a request, which actually pertains also to me, and that is that we need to pay attention and make pauses between question and answer so that the interpreters could do their job properly. At the very beginning of the cross-examination, Mr. Babic, we mentioned the founding of the Croatian Democratic Community at the beginning of 1989 in Croatia. Was that the time that this happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when it was but it was established before the law on parties was adopted, I think, so it was sometime in 1989. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We also mentioned the HDZ Assembly held at the Lisinski hall on the 24th of February 1990, when the introductory speech was given by Mr. Tudjman, stating the party's programme. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We also mentioned a sentence from Mr. Tudjman's speech on that day in February 1990, which stated - I'm paraphrasing - the independent Republic of Croatia was not only a quisling creation and a fascist crime but it was also an expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people. Do you recall that sentence, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the HDZ Assembly sent an appeal -- or the actual party, the HDZ party, appealed to the citizens of Croatia on the eve of the first multi-party elections in April 1990, in which it called every citizen to vote for a sovereign and independent Croatia, within its natural borders, which more or less encompassed also parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that during the election campaign, the HDZ favoured an independent Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that along with that position, about the need to create an independent sovereign Republic of or state of Croatia which up until then was part of the Yugoslav federation, so along with that programme, there was also -- there were also steps taken to change the Croatian constitution and thereby change the position of the Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One thing was the election campaign. The elections or the second round of elections was completed in late May, or rather, the second round was held on the 8th and the elections were completed by the end of May, while the initiative to change the constitution was made after the new Croatian Assembly was constituted, and this was sometime in late June or early July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid any misunderstandings, which year are we talking about? We are talking about April, May, June; which year was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We've already talked to the proposed amendments to the then Croatian constitution and we also talked about -- or you talked about how representatives of the Serb people in Croatia objected to these amendments and ultimately rejected them at the Srb Sabor; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Assembly in Srb was held on the 25th of July 1990; is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We also mentioned that the Assembly in Srb was proclaimed as an Assembly of the Serbian people and Croatia -- and that's where the Serbian National Council was also formed as a representative body of the Serbian people in Croatia; is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We also talked about how the Serbian National Council, as the executive body of the Serb Assembly, scheduled a referendum of the Serbian people in Croatia on autonomy from the 19th of August until the 2nd of September 1990. Is this correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We also talked about how the Croatian Assembly declared as illegal that referendum of the Serbian people in Croatia and that as of the 18th of August onwards, it sent special Croatian police units to confiscate weapons at the police stations in the territory of the Krajina; is this correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it misstates the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Maybe before I ask you to say something, Mr. Milovancevic, Mr. Whiting, can you indicate in what respect is the testimony being misstated?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour. I didn't understand -- I mean, the Defence counsel has said we talked about but -- which makes his formulations a little ambiguous but I didn't understand Mr. Babic to testify that from the 18th of August onwards, special Croatian police units were sent to confiscate weapons at the police stations in the territory of Krajina. The testimony is a little more complex than that. And I don't think that that summary is accurate. Perhaps if Defence counsel has a reference, we could check it, and I could be -- I could stand corrected but I think it's more complicated than that; that there was -- I think the testimony is that there was information about special police units being sent, that information turned out not to be true, separately there was an effort on the part of the Croatian government to centralise weapons that were being held, and I think confiscate weapons is perhaps not the right term. So I think two different things are being conflated here and an inaccurate term is being used. That's my recollection of the testimony, but I can stand corrected if there is a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is yesterday's transcript, line 22, where Mr. Babic, in response to my question -- well, I can formulate the question differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line 22 of what page of yesterday's testimony, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 15, Your Honour, line 22. Pages 15 and 16 on the -- on page 16, the number on the upper right corner is number 16, line 22. That's the part of the testimony that I was thinking of. It's at the very bottom of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is it page 15 or page 16, line 22?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 16. Page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's clear in that answer that there are two different events that are being talked about. One is about information having to do with special police units being sent, and this is a separate issue that's being talked about with weapons being confiscated not by special police units, and the witness was careful to say they should be centralised rather than confiscation, so I think it is different from what -- how counsel represented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't understand what the problem is. If I understood the witness in a way that differs from what he actually said, then the witness can explain that. The witness is here. I'm just presenting to him, based on what he said yesterday, the question, and I think it's quite specific and precise and brief, and he can always respond. I also need to note that we are wasting time, in a way, with these objections by the Prosecutor, and then also the Prosecutor is presenting the answer before the witness has had a chance to answer. So in a way the Prosecutor is suggesting the answer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest that I've been very restrained in my objections, and the problem from the point of view of the Prosecution, is that it is improper for Defence counsel to mischaracterise what the witness has said either in earlier answers in cross-examination or in his direct testimony. That's simply improper. If he wants to put the question a different way, if he wants to go over the testimony again and again, the same questions, he can do that, but he has an obligation to put -- to characterise the witness's prior testimony accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, so that we can make progress, we are going to deal with these issues one by one, okay? The first is the objection that you are misquoting the evidence, and if you want to raise an objection that the Prosecution is wasting time, do so after we've dealt with this one, okay? Now, I have no way of seeing both of these transcripts simultaneously. Let me see if I can. It's disappeared on the other screen. But certainly, as I remember what you said now, Mr. Milovancevic, what I read at the bottom of page 16 is not verbatim with what you have said. There is -- well, there is a -- the word "confiscate" is used there but it's used in a question, as I see it, and not in an answer, so I would request you to read the answer as you got it at page 16: "I said that I did have some information about the events that took place. I said that I wasn't sure whether it was exactly on the 17th or around that time, but there was a decision by the Croatian government and the MUP for the weapons of the police reserve forces, which happened to be in the police stations, should be collected and placed in other locations. So that was the reason why the Croatian MUP confiscated the weapons and moved them to different locations, which I don't know what they were." The word is used in an explanatory form. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you read the text from the transcript. I was not making any kind of assertion of my own. I simply asked the witness whether that was the gist of his answer from yesterday or not. And whether he can help us with that and give us an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection was basically that in giving him the gist, you misrepresented. You may proceed [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Better still, ask questions rather than repeat his evidence to him, because there is this problem of misquoting it or not misquoting it. Just ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, yesterday you mentioned the Balvan revolution, the log revolution. And you mentioned the action by the Croatian police relating to the seizure of weapons, as you said confiscation of weapons, and my question is: This confiscation of weapons by the Croatian SUP, does that have anything to do with the referendum of the Serbian people in Krajina that was scheduled?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was quite specific about that, that there were two problems which were being resolved. One of them was the political issue of organising the referendum, which the Croatian government described as illegal. Then this referendum was changed as an expression of views instead of a referendum, and it was included in the constitutional norms. That was one problem. The second problem was the fact that some police stations refused obedience in some municipalities in Knin. That was the second problem. The third problem, whether it's distinct or it had something to do with the refusal of obedience of the police officer was the storing of weapons of the reserve police forces to other locations. So I think that I responded to each one of these matters and explained them in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, whether the MUP of Croatia stored weapons in special warehouses only on the territories of the Serb territory municipalities or all over?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation that was given by the MUP of Croatia was that it related to the whole of Croatia. However, this was seen in Serb municipalities as a problem which was a problem of those municipalities alone or, rather, the police in those particular municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that the MUP of Croatia wanted to place that under their control at locations that were accessible to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a public announcement or statement that you issued after a meeting with the delegation of the Croatian parliament, Mr. Degoricija and a delegation of the MUP of Croatia, Mr. Boljkovac on the one hand and you and other Serb representatives on the other. And you said that you issued a statement on the 10th of September 1990 about that; isn't that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that statement, do you establish the starting points for calming the situation and dealing with the tensions and along with agreement that all problems be settled with the institutions concerned, both political and socio-economical ones and that political issues be settled by interparty agreement? Do you remember a text to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did it also say in that statement that in order to implement the agreement, that both sides wished to return the weapons to the reserve forces, to their primary state, and that the ultimatum for the return of weapons be deferred and that the Croatian ministry should launch the initiative in the Croatian parliament to have the SUP returned to Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also say that the Serbs refused to return the weapons and that that's why the agreement fell through?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian parliament move an initiative and decide to set up the SUP in Knin as had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think that there was a letter to that effect by Pecerski, who was a MUP official who attended the meeting and that an initiative along those lines was in fact made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When and who from the MUP Sabor or MUP of Croatia established that the agreement with respect to the return of weapons fell through, since a deadline had not been set, that this was a process, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that after that, there was an escalation of tensions and provocations and general unrest, so that in fact the crisis was caused -- I meant Boro Mikelic, the popular militia, and so on. The tensions had escalated to such an extent that the federal organs had to involve themselves in solving the crisis. Vasil Tupurkovski, a member of the Yugoslav state Presidency arrived, for instance, as did the representatives of the federal organs, and as I said, after that, the crisis escalated. It came to a head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The agreement that you mentioned was on the 9th or 10th of September 1990, was it not, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May we show on the overhead projector 65 ter Exhibit number 43. Unless I'm much mistaken, Your Honour, that should be a transcript of a cassette of an intercept of Mr. Spegelj, and the transcript of that intercepted conversation exists in English. It is the one Mr. Spegelj had with the minister of the interior of Croatia, Josip Boljkovac, on the 14th of October, the 19th of October, and the 16th of December 1990. And that transcript or, rather, the sound track was heard in the well-known film about General Spegelj. I have the transcript under number 43, Exhibit number 43, on the list of -- 65 ter list of Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Somebody is trying to check that for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before, in order to save time, Your Honour, the transcript appears on our monitors, I'd like to ask

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does he remember the film about General Spegelj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was from January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the film, excerpts were shown of intercepted conversations linked to the plans of Mr. Spegelj, General Spegelj, and the import of weapons? And do you remember a specific sentence uttered by Mr. Spegelj, and in the transcript it says that that was uttered on the 14th of October 1990: "At the critical moment, find two or three men who will come to the most dangerous parts -- they should be eliminated physically. He sent someone to the flat, he appears at the door, bang, bang, bang, and he goes down the stairs, he goes to the next flat, then you deal with the next person, and so on. The most dangerous people must be killed on their thresholds regardless of the women and children." Do you remember that kind of sentence, that portion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that and that we were shown a picture of Spegelj talking to someone, some people. It was filmed in a room of some kind, and also he talked to Boljkovac in a car. And you could understand some of the things he said and other things appeared as the transcript underneath the image is shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. I hope that we'll find the exhibit in question but what I'm putting to you now is a translation of the participants in the talk, Mr. Spegelj and Mr. Boljkovac. On that same day, according to the transcript given us by the Prosecution, on the 14th of October 1990, Spegelj, while talking -- or rather, while talking he says the following: "That will be war. It will be a civil war in which there will be no mercy shown to anyone, either towards the women or to the children. In the family flats, quite simply hand grenades." Do you remember a text like that? I don't wish to repeat it word by word, but do you remember the general contents of the footage shown?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of October 1990, according to the transcript, which was compiled on the basis of the conversation intercepted, Spegelj says: "There is nothing here for the army. It will be completely destroyed. Five men are covering each of the -- each office in Virovitica. They will be massacred already at their homes." Then there is an interruption in the sentence and he goes on to say, "None of them will be allowed to reach the barracks. On the street --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, I just ask, could we know what page of the transcript counsel is reading from? I'm just -- it's a -- I just want to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this transcript has been provided to us in English, as I say, within the 65 ter exhibits, Exhibit 43, two pages long, the 14th of October and the 19th of October, and December. Those are the dates and pages. And the 14th of October conversation is on the second page. So it's just two pages of that transcript, page 1 and page 2. What I read from, that last sentence, in Virovitica, about five-to-one officer, that nobody must be allowed to reach the barracks, that's on page 1 towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have 65 ter Exhibit 43 up and it's a 22-page document and it doesn't correspond to what counsel is talking about. I don't know where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have a problem, Mr. Milovancevic. It looks like we are not looking at the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are two documents with the contents of the film and the intercept between Mr. Spegelj and Mr. Boljkovac. One document is a complete one and in its entirety it has 23 pages, and then on those 23 pages or within those pages you'll find the dates that I mentioned. However, when I say number 43, that's the document number and document we received from the Prosecution pursuant to the 65 ter list, and that exhibit, of those 23 pages, has just these two pages with the four dates. So the document that I read from contains just those four dates and four sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you at that point, Mr. Milovancevic. The fact of the matter is on the screen we've got a 22-page document. You're talking of a two-page document. Maybe before you can proceed you should try to make sure that we have the same document. If the two-page document is a summary of the 22-page document, let us have the two-page document on the screen. Then when we talk of pages we know we are on the same page, indeed. But as it is now, I'm also having a document with 22 pages. Let's sort that out first. Court officials, are you able to help us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised, Mr. Milovancevic, that the Court officials only have the 22-page document and not the two-page document. You will have to use the 22-page document so that we are all on a wavelength. If you can find that and refer us to that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first conversation, which relates to the 14th of October 1990, in which Spegelj and Boljkovac are talking, is to be found on pages 22 and 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- and 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, to avoid wasting time, I can continue examining the witness, continue with my cross-examination, and in the meantime, we'll find the exact dates and the exact pages which will make it easier for us to identify it and to have the same documents in front of us, but I would like to ask him a few more questions related to the documents and then we can go back to the documents themselves or, rather, the transcripts and the individual dates, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is that the Prosecution has asked you to give them a reference of exactly where you are because, when you were asking your questions, they didn't know what you were talking about. They were looking at a 22-page document, you were looking at a two-page document. I suggest that we get the correct pages, that is at page 22 -- I'm waiting for the document to come on the screen. You can go on page 22 and you can ask the questions. Can we get the document on the screen? Right. We are on page 22 of the document, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 22 and 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't have 23, Mr. Milovancevic. I have only 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 22, at the bottom of that page, we have a sentence which reads -- the last sentence: "Listen, if the need arises in a crucial moment, find two or three men to get rid of the most dangerous ones."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conversation of the 19th of October 1990, which I mentioned, and which I put to the witness, is to be found on page 18. Can we take a look at page 18 now, please? Page 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, let's look at the text. The last words of Martin Spegelj, there is a text underneath those words, and you can stop here. Here, Martin Spegelj is talking on the 19th of October 1990, and he says, Mr. Babic: "There is nothing for the army there. It will be defeated badly." A few lines below that, Martin Spegelj again says: "Every officer is covered with five men in Virovitica and they are all going to be executed while still at their homes." And this is the text that I put to you, Mr. Babic. This is on page 18. On page 13, there is another part of the intercept recorded on the 16th of December. Can we have that on the screen, please? Page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are done with page 18? You're not asking any questions on page 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 13? Can you scroll up until we see the date, the date is 16th December 1990. Very well. Stop. Scroll down, please. Scroll down. Just a little. That's okay now. On this page, Mr. Boljkovac, the minister of the interior of Croatia, says as follows: "We are going to use all means. We are going to use weapons and the Serbs in Croatia will never be what they have been so far. Their supremacy is history. Their Knin is not going to be Knin any more. We will take over Knin. Knin is going to disappear."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this part of the conversation in the film featuring Martin Spegelj which was recorded in January 1991, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember. This was rather intimidating, very scary for all of us, and this is one part of that film from January 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the transcript and in the film, you could see what the plans of the Croatian leadership was, the leadership of the police and the state already in October 1990. Was that immediately after your meeting with Boljkovac and Degoricija, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question? Was that recorded? Was there a conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether this conversation in October 1990 took place immediately after the conversation that you had with them in September?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when the conversation took place. It was shown in January 1991 and our conversation took place on the 10th of September, and what you're quoting here is indeed October and November. It took place in October and November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Did you also state that after the conversation that took place in September, and once the preparations for the changes of the Croatian constitution went on, did you personally propose to the parliament to have SAO Krajina as a county and that was denied?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted SAO Krajina to be given the status of a county, and it was refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on 19 September -- December 1990, there was the proclamation of SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 21st of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. 21st of December 1990. We mean 1990, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the provisions of the Statute, was SAO Krajina an autonomous region within the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who is General Spegelj? Can you tell us? Just briefly. Do you know anything about his position before this conversation and after this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January, and probably even earlier, I don't know as of when, he was the minister of defence in the government of Croatia. Earlier on he was a JNA general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is Mr. Boljkovac the minister of the interior with whom you had a conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It was in September 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This film, was it shown in January 1991 and he spoke about -- Spegelj spoke about illegal import of weapons into Croatia, and is that why it was so sensational?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about the illegal import of arms and threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you state that the Presidency of Yugoslavia in mid-January 1991 made a decision that all the surplus of illegally seized weapons should be returned and that the reserve police should be disbanded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that on the 9th of January the Presidency made the decision that the reserve police force should be reduced to the regular strength, and that all the paramilitary formations should be disbanded. That was the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in March 1991, there were first armed conflicts in Pakrac between the special police force of Croatia and the Serb police in Pakrac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a conflict, yes. I don't know who the participants in the conflict were. I only know what I read in the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. That will do. Are you aware of the fact although you stated that yesterday that the proposal of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in mid-March 1999 [as interpreted] was to introduce martial law but that it was denied at the Presidency meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with that, did you mention the session of the Presidency of Yugoslavia which took place on the 12th, 14th and 15th of March? This was a dramatic session at which this decision was not passed. Is that the event that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This session took place at the headquarters of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. After that, there was another conflict in Plitvice on the 31st of March 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that both in Pakrac and in Plitvice, pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the JNA intervened and separated the two parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we mentioned the events in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May 1991. You said that you don't know any details. I'm asking you now whether you have any general information as to the fact that the JNA intervened there in order to separate the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you mentioned Borovo Selo in the context of removing barricades at the beginning of April 1991, that you didn't mention the 2nd of May. According to my information, and I do have some information, on the events that took place on the 2nd of May. And yesterday your question was about what happened there in April and about the barricades, if I understood your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. On the 2nd of May, was there an armed conflict in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the parties to that conflict were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the one side there was the Croatian police and on the other side the -- the local Serbs, Seselj's Chetniks, and Frenki's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA intervene in Borovo Selo and did they prevent further conflicts and casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with Mr. Dzakula about the events in Borovo Selo? He is a native of that area.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzakula is not a native of Borovo Selo but of Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I meant the general region of Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to the people from Eastern Slavonia about this incident later on, but not with Dzakula.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Are you familiar with the speech of General Tudjman in Trogir at the beginning of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a speech. I believe that this took place after the events in Split, or about those events at the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the chronology that I'm aware of, first Mr. Tudjman spoke in Trogir and after that, there was a large scale protest of citizens in Split and the strangling of the soldier Sasko Gesovski. Do you remember that image from the TV?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is something that was broadcast rather often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us what happened in Split. What do you know about the incident in Split?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what I heard and saw in the media, and I don't know exactly what happened because I don't have any precise information, save for what was broadcast on TV and what was written in the media. There was an attack. I don't know who attacked whom; the Croatian citizens, the members of the HDZ attacked the command of the JNA there. This is where the conflict took place. One soldier got killed and the one who was strangled, he wasn't killed. He didn't die. But the image was rather dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Under such circumstances, on the 12th and on the 19th of May, something happened. What happened on the 12th and what happened on the 19th of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, after this incident, Croats mostly voted for the independence of Croatia, and on the 12th of May, Serbs in the SAO Krajina staged their referendum and they voted for staying with Serbia, Montenegro, and other republics that wanted to preserve Yugoslavia as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened after that in June, on the 25th of June 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian parliament proclaimed the independence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the same day, did Slovenia pass an identical decision? The Republic of Slovenia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia proclaimed such decisions against the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: After a very short armed conflict in Slovenia, where units of the JNA that had been dispatched by the federal government in order to restore the constitutional order of Yugoslavia, those units were attacked and there was a decision on the temporary withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia; isn't that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There is another thing that happened in July. That was the Brioni memorandum or the moratorium on the decisions of Slovenia and Croatia on secession; is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "moratorium," you're talking about the decision to defer the implementation of those decisions, the decisions on the independence of Croatia and Slovenia, by three months. In other words, there would have been a deferral of three months to those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. From the first multi-party elections in April 1991, in Croatia, until the decision made by Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia on the 25th of June 1991, can you tell us what the position of the Serbs as citizens of Croatia was? Were there any changes there? I don't know whether I was clear enough. I'm talking about the attitude towards the Serbs, the way they were treated, the conditions of life, the way they were treated at work, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several stages in the development of those relationships. In different parts of Croatia, the situation differed. At the beginning, until January and February, the situation was that I approached the Commission of -- for Human Rights in Geneva and I spoke about the violation of the rights of Serbs until then. Serbs were being fired from their jobs, especially from the state-held positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you said February, but you didn't mention the year. When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1991. That was one situation. Generally speaking, that is. After that, we already spoke about incidents in some parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Can you tell us about people being fired from work? Who fired whom and in what services and institutions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I had, there were some companies that were closed, and then the workers were taken back again, but Serbs were not. What was specific, though, was the dismissal of Serbs from public institutions, especially from government institutions and from the police. I think that the position of the Croatian government was quite precise; that there were too many Serbs in the staff of those institutions in relation to the overall population. That was a characteristic occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. This policy of dismissal of Serbs, was that implemented in relation to Serbs only because of their ethnicity? Did you speak about that in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was -- I just felt that that was a violation of the Serbs' basic human rights, or civil rights, because they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in that period President Tudjman's statement, as president of the HDZ and the president of Croatia, that he was happy that his wife was not Jewish or Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was quoted, this was something that was frequently cited as his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I made a mistake. It's still too early for the break. We still have 15 minutes to go. I apologise, Your Honours. I just thought that it was already time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just before you go on, is the witness aware of what nationality the wife actually was? Or what ethnic group she belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tudjman's wife?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was generally known, at least based on the media information, that she was Croatian, but I never met her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Along with the problems of the Serbs because they were being dismissed from their jobs, were there any issues relating to some statements of loyalty?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statements of loyalty, that was something that started in the spring, in March and April of 1991, through the trade unions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Mr. Babic, what the gist of that request was, and how did the Serbs understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the gist was for them to accept Croatia as their state. That's what it was about. The entire time that Croatia was disassociating itself from Yugoslavia, Krajina was disassociating itself from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And how did the Serb population understand such a request by the new Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Besides the pressure that the Serb population in Croatia was exposed to, could you please tell us what the position of the Yugoslav People's Army in Croatia was. What was the position of the JNA and its members there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what the general position was of the Croatian government. I think that I mentioned once that the position was that the Yugoslav People's Army should not interfere in the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis. That was the position of the Croatian government. When the Yugoslav People's Army did participate in this resolution, then the Croatian government began to blockade the JNA facilities in order to keep the army inside these facilities so that it would not be engaged in the political settling of accounts. Finally, in late August, there was open warfare between the JNA, and the JNA began offensive operations against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And how were the JNA facilities in Croatia blockaded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can talk about that based on what I read or heard in the media. These were blockades consisting of citizens, police, the guards, and so on. Barricades were erected using cars on the exits to these buildings or facilities. Later this escalated in summer or early in the fall, when water and electricity were cut off, and then it ultimately led to warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with the JNA columns that were with drawing from Slovenia through Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the JNA was withdrawing from Slovenia using trains and also moving along coastal roads. One of these trains was captured, but I'm not quite sure exactly what happened. I heard that it had been captured and held in Croatia but I don't know exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who captured this column with weapons? Were these Croatian authorities or someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about explosions which were occurring throughout Dalmatia and in other places where Serb-owned facilities were blown up? This was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, I think in May or around that time, May 1991, there were two incidents where buildings were demolished. In Zadar, the HDZ, or Croats, I don't know who, destroyed Serbian facilities. The second incident was in Knin, where the Serbs were demolishing buildings belonging to Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that international institutions mentioned the figure of 10.000 blown-up Serb houses and businesses in that period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure but what I said actually gives an illustration of that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about disappearances of ethnic Serbs from their apartments while they were on their way back home from work or disappearing from the streets or being taken in without warrants?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the press wrote about the case of the Zec family in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the Zec family in Zagreb, and when was this, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you precisely when, but it was during the conflict. It was probably in 1991. There were articles in the press about how the Serb family Zec was taken from its apartment and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who was killed of that family?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I really couldn't tell you anything specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that there was a child, a girl, 12 or 13 years old from the Zec family who was raped and then killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically. All I remember is that there were articles about the Zec family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about whether the perpetrators were found and punished? Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I heard later, somebody was charged for that, but I don't know if they were ever arrested. I know the trial wasn't ever finished. Maybe they escaped. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear information that this -- in this incident people from Mr. Tudjman's security actually were involved in the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what happened on the Korani bridge. This is something that is quite known to you, probably. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, it was in any case before wide-scale combat began, a group of reservists on their way to the barracks in Karlovac or Logoriste, I don't know exactly, was intercepted by the Croatian police or guards, and I think that they were all killed, or the majority of them were killed at the Korani bridge or in Karlovci -- Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about -- anything about them being tortured before they were killed, that this was a pretty brutal murder and that some of them jumped off the bridge in order to survive?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I read the account of one survivor, who did describe the event in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the disappearances of people in Sisak from the summer of 1991? And did you hear anything about the number of these people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was Sisak. There is a Serbian village called Kinjacka near Sisak. Several Serb civilians were killed there by the Croatian armed forces, or formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the period of 1991, does the name Pakracka Poljana mean anything to you, or the facilities there? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to information, the Croatian police, most probably, and Mercep is being mentioned as the executioner of Serbs from that area, I think that even The Hague Tribunal investigated this incident, according to some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did this involve the arrest of ethnic Serbs just because they were Serbs, without any court order or warrant, their being taken to specially prepared camps where they were severely beaten, tortured, and then finally liquidated and that the figure is several hundred such people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the information was but I don't know anything specifically. I don't know whether the investigation was completed about these events. There was information later that the bodies were relocated somewhere in Lika but I don't know anything other than what I read from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the hijacking or kidnapping and killing of a group of Serbs from Gospic; and do you know approximately when this happened in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the summer of 1991, a group of Serb civilians was taken from Gospic and they were killed near Gospic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these judges, prosecutors, police officers, respected Serb figures who were killed in a brutal way? The exhumations later indicated that they had sustained quite serious injuries?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that besides the bodies that were found, the bodies of Serb victims, there was also a figure of 125 Serbs who had been kidnapped from Gospic and no traces -- there were no traces of them later once -- after they disappeared?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This figure was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about who the perpetrators of all of these crimes that we mentioned so far were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Croatian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this would be a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned some events from 1991, Mr. Babic. Now, do you know anything about the suffering of or, rather, the destruction of the Serb villages Bestrma and Cakale in Banija in August 1991, some sort of execution expedition which passed by that way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the area of Kinjacka. I don't know whether that's nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. We mentioned the import of weapons, illegal import of weapons, into Croatia, and this subject was dealt with in the film about Martin Spegelj. We also mentioned a Presidency decision by which all the weapon surpluses should be collected together. Do you happen to know when the Croatian National Guards Corps, the ZNG in abbreviation, came to be formed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about the creation of the Croatian National Guards Corps. I don't think I can give you a very precise date when it was established but it was spring of 1991 certainly, perhaps by, say, May or June. I think that's when the Croatian National Guards Corps was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a review of the units that was held at the football stadium, I think, at the Maksimir football stadium, I think, in Zagreb, in May, 1991, May or June?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that that was roughly the time when they were established, or when they appeared in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian National Guards Corps, did that mean the beginning of a new Croatian army? Were those the seeds of a new Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think officially it was defined as a police force of the Ministry of Defence, but actually it was the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did this take place in 1991, at the time when Yugoslavia was a single state, when it had a single armed force, one Territorial Defence, when the Yugoslav constitution was in force and the federal laws and when the establishment of formations of that kind was not legally possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Well, I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question, Mr. Milovancevic. You say, Did this take place in 1991? What took place in 1991? The full question is: "Did this take place in 1991, at a time when Yugoslavia was a single state, when it had a single armed force, one Territorial Defence, when the Yugoslavia constitution was in force and the federal laws and when the establishment of formations of that kind was not legally possible." What --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand your question, Your Honour. Thank you for asking that question. I cut the question in half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The creation of the new Croatian armed forces and units, did that happen when the federal constitution on the territory of Yugoslavia was still in force?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was at the time when Croatia had proclaimed that it would settle what it owed to Yugoslavia and proclaim its independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This separation, was it a unilateral act on the part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll have to give you a longer answer in order to be able to ask your question -- answer your question about this disassociation. The declaration on disassociation was a document that Croatia proclaimed on, I think it was the 20th of February, on the disassociation of Croatia, and this was a conditional disassociation, that is to say separation from Yugoslavia as a condition. And after the referendum, Croatia, in the referendum of May 1991, proclaimed its independence. However, how did this referendum come about? And this is the answer to your question whether it was unilateral. The referendum came about on the basis of an agreement between the presidents of the republics of Yugoslavia who had taken part in settling and resolving the crises, that is to say referendums were held both in Croatia and in Krajina, and they were the product of an agreement between the presidents of the republics of Yugoslavia so that it was, as I say, a product or the result, shall I say, of an agreement as to how the crisis should be solved on the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. I understand what you're saying. The Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, at the request of the federal government in mid-1991, all the decisions of Croatia and Slovenia linked to secession, did it proclaim them unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something along those lines, I've already said, roughly speaking, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We also mentioned the situation when the European Community became involved in settling the Yugoslav crisis and the Brioni memorandum of the 7th and 8th of July 1991. And I think you said that the memorandum provided for a three-month pause during which time the republics of Slovenia and Croatia would not go ahead with their decision to secede. Is that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the agreement also provide for the fact that other steps would also be taken which would lead to a political settlement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The substance of it was to find a political solution to the crisis, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this three-month deadline, that is to say the 7th and 8th of 1991, or rather that it expired on the 8th of October 1991, would that be it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croatian armed formations in the course of September 1991 took up a series of very large barracks, amongst other places in Slavonia, in Bjelovar, in Virovitica, for example, as well as Varazdin and other places? Did you hear about that happening?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think that Tudjman himself made statements to that effect at the time, when he said that the Knin Corps still remained out of control, of all the other corps in Croatia, at that time or somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So when the Croatian leadership pledged to the European Community that it would stop and not go ahead with its decision for a certain period of time, it went ahead and took over the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the real war against the JNA began -- or with the JNA, began in August, and up until then, as I've already said, there was a blockade of the various facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the suffering of the population of Western Slavonia during the operations of the Croatian armed forces that took place in October, November and December 1991 and the cleansing of 192 Serb settlements?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about those events, with the proviso that the events were a little more complicated, I seem to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a document placed on the monitor. It is 1D0019, a Defence document. The document is the book by Dr. Zdravko Tomac. "Behind Closed Doors" is the title. Before we see the document on our monitors, I should like to ask that 65 ter Exhibit 43 be tendered into evidence. It is the intercept on 22 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have an objection with the understanding that there were only very small portions of those 22 pages that were talked about, and were discussed by the witness. There are only -- my recollection is of the 22 pages, only two or three pages, so I have no objection to the exhibit going in with the understanding that it is for the purpose of those portions that were discussed by the witness and not the other portions of the document which relate to other matters -- well, relate to other intercepts or other things, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. The document will be admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 237, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you know that on the 3rd or 4th of August 1991, in Croatia, after the elections, the first government of democratic unity was formed? That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, roughly at that time. I don't know the exact date, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Dr. Zdravko Tomac was one of the vice-presidents of that government, or vice-premier; the Prime Minister was Dr. Greguric. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about Tomac but I do know that he was one of the officials. What his post actually was, or his title, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can have the monitor -- the document placed on the monitor, on the overhead projector by Dr. Tomac, "Behind Closed Doors" is the title, I would like us to turn to page 55 in the Serbian version and it is 1D00-0153 is the number of it. Otherwise, it is page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I the only one who is lost? I seem to be having --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the document appears on the monitor, Mr. Babic, not to waste time, I'm going to ask you a few questions. Did the Yugoslav People's Army, as the federal armed force in the entire post-war period from 1945, that is, until 1991, exist, with all its garrisons, all its units and facilities, throughout the territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the distribution of the garrisons, the warehouses and outposts of the JNA? Was that something that was structured on the basis of federal provisions for the whole of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Yugoslav constitution, did the Yugoslav state Presidency, as a collective president, or rather was it the Supreme Commander of the armed forces in peacetime and the Supreme Command with the federal secretary of national defence as a staff of the Supreme Command in wartime?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And the Yugoslav People's Army as a federal armed force, did it have a highly developed system of education and training for officers, training them for their own requirements; and those military schools and academies, did they exist both in Belgrade and Zagreb and Split and other towns?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As for the enrolment of candidates for officers, was that allowed to everybody regardless of their affiliation; religious or ethnic, that is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the JNA, as the federal armed force, was considered and behaved as the guardsman of fraternity and unity of all peoples, regardless of their national, ethnic, or religious background?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the leaderships of Croatia, Slovenia in 1991, before and after the decision on secession, invited members of the Croatian people and the Slovenian people not to serve in the JNA? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're talking about is something that was quite well known. And there were two processes. One process was of officers leaving the JNA and joining the national armies, and the second process was replacement of Serbian and -- staff by the Slovenian and Croatian staff. That is another part of the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in addition to the army General Kadijevic, a number of key positions in the JNA was reserved for members of all the Yugoslav peoples; the Macedonians, the Slovenes, the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we know what time period we are talking about here? Because I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The period in question is when the crisis in Yugoslavia escalated. That is May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up until May, there was the so-called ethnic distribution in the JNA and the staff was employed according to the ethnic structure; i.e., the ethnic structure amongst the general population of Yugoslavia, more or less so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have said that pursuant to the decision of the Yugoslav top leadership, first there was a blockade of JNA barracks and then those barracks were attacked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about the evolvement of conflict with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that that -- during the Brioni moratorium, during the period between the 8th of July and the 8th of October, when all the processes were supposed to be frozen, there was an attack on a number of barracks and a lot of military equipment was captured by the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time there were two distinct periods. The first one ends with the end of August. At that time, the JNA was in a way passive, so to say, and played a role of a body that separated the party to the conflict; and after the end of August, it became an active participant in the conflict that you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the clarity, you mentioned the month of August. What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since the document that we asked for did not appear on the monitor, in order not to waste too much time, I would now like to have the following document on the screen: 65 ter Exhibit number 1227. And before the document appears on the screen, I'm going to tell you, Mr. Babic, that this is a report or an order of the command of the 1st Military District, dated 19 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My associates are telling me that the previous document has just appeared on the screen. I would like to go back to that document, if I may. Can we discuss Mr. Tomac's book? If I'm allowed to do so, I would like to go back to the document, which is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You would be allowed to do that, Mr. Milovancevic, if we can get it on our screen as well. We still have the spiral thing. Okay. We now have it in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, we will have on our screen page 3 of the English version and this is the translation of page 55 of the original of Mr. Tomac's book, and the marking is 1D00-0153. Can we have that page on the screen, please. Can we have the page in question on the screen, please? If we can get the page, then I would like to proceed. If not, I will proceed with another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. We have a B/C/S copy on the screen, on our screen. Is it possible to get an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the screen we now have page 55 of Mr. Tomac's book. The page is in B/C/S, and for the Trial Chamber it would be good if we could have page 3 of the English translation of that same text. If possible. If not, then we can maybe -- I believe that we have the English version on the screen, and the page is number 3. On page number 3 of the translation of Mr. Tomac's book, at the very top, there is a passage in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, could you please turn to that passage 3 that will be shown to you, and the -- can you scroll up the B/C/S text to show passage number 3? Thank you. That's it. Mr. Tomac, on this page, page 55 of the B/C/S version of his book, which is page 3 in English, says: "That is why in our strategy it was very important to precisely establish the rules of behaviour towards the Yugoslav People's Army, how to act to neutralise it and for it to become a purely Serbian, Montenegrin army as late as possible." I am reading just part of the text, which is a lengthy one. Mr. Babic, did I read the text correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did. I can see that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And now, can we have on the screen page 56 of this book. Again it is on page 3 of the English translation. This is 1D00-0154. Do you see the text on page 54, where Mr. -- 56, where Mr. Tomac says: "The following stage, in order to win the international support and to prevent the JNA from getting involved in the war against Slovenia and Croatia was to advocate the confederal option and accepting a long-term negotiation, although it was well known that the negotiations would eventually fall through"? Can you see that text on the screen, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this text, does Mr. Tomac, as a Vice-Prime Minister of the Croatian government, talks about the negotiations that were staged just to buy time, although it was well known that the negotiations would eventually fall through? Is that the meaning of this passage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what he means, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. And now can we have on the screen page number 81 in B/C/S. This is 1D00-0178. The English translation is still on page 3 of the translation. On this page, Mr. Babic, it says somewhere in the middle of the text: "On the 4th of August, 1991, the parliament was given to know the new government, the government of democratic unity, in the following composition: Dr. Franjo Greguric, Prime Minister; Dr. Mato Granic, Dr. Milan Ramljak, Dr. Zdravko Tomac, vice-presidents. Mr. Tomac, who was the -- one of the vice-presidents of the government, is the author of this book. Does it say in this passage that Mr. Tomac was indeed a Vice-Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 84 on the screen, the middle of that page in B/C/S. This is page 1D00-0181. And the translation of this page is on page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the interpreters do not have the English version on their screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to get an English version for the interpreters on their screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have this problem as well. The interpreters have only the monitor, the Court monitor, which has the B/C/S version. They do not have the separate monitor which has the English version. If Defence counsel has a hard copy - that's what we did - that could be provided to the interpreters and it would be of assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are the interpreters not able to interpret what they see in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that just presents a difficulty for them. I'll let them speak for themselves, but my understanding is that trying to do that kind of interpretation is difficult and what they prefer to have is the text that's already been interpreted so that they have that to assist them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. If you're able to help the interpreters with a hard copy, Mr. Milovancevic, are you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour I have just one copy. I did not expect this problem. Otherwise, I would be only glad to give a copy to the interpreters because it is in our best interests for this to be as expeditious as possible, although the passages are very brief, the ones that we are going to use, so if the interpreters would be so kind as to interpret from the B/C/S that they have on the monitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Then may we ask, then, the interpreters to be so kind as to try and interpret from the B/C/S that they have on their monitors. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have come to page 83. I believe that I have given you the number in B/C/S, and on the screen we have page 84. Can we scroll back to page 83, please. On page 83, somewhere in the middle of the first passage, Mr. Tomac says, "Because of the Brioni moratorium, Croatia could not pass a law on national defence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could you go a little slower because of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: "Due to the Brioni moratorium, Croatia could not pass a law on national defence. It could not organise its own military. That is why we were forced until the moment the Brioni moratorium expired, to look for solutions out of the institutions in order to organise our defence. That is why the Croatian military was being created within the Ministry of the Interior and the police." Is this what it says in this text, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is this in keeping with the information that you are aware of, you have spoken about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we see page 84 on the screen now, the middle of the page, the marking is 1D00-0181, and in the English it's still on page 3. In the middle of the paragraph that's marked with number 2, on page 84 of the B/C/S version, Mr. Tomac says: "War was never declared and proclaimed in Croatia. We could not declare it and proclaim it. We waged war against the federal state, whose laws we formally had to implement, so that we had to seek ways how not to implement them, how to gradually dismantle them and practically in an illegal way how to create our own state, until the expiration of the Brioni moratorium in the beginning of October." Is that the text on page 84, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 85 on the monitor, in the B/C/S. Marking is 1D00-01812, and it's is it still on page 2 -- on page 3 of the English translation. In this text, Mr. Babic, Mr. Tomac explained how this was done during the Brioni moratorium, and he says -- it's at the top of the page, page 85: "That is why we had to act in three ways: A, create certain institutions, parallel with state organs (regional Crisis Staffs as a concentration of civilian and military power in wartime conditions, organising the defence within the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the police and not the Ministry of Defence). "B, certain defence tasks were to be implemented outside of the state institutions, which could not be trusted because of the infiltration of those who were waging war against us. Thus, some important tasks were implemented through the ruling party and trust worthy, reliable people, (the procurement and distribution of weapons and ammunition, organising special purpose production, and so on). "C, prepare all laws and organisation for the day when the moratorium would be abolished on the implementation of the decision on the declaration of an independent and sovereign Croatian state."
