Is this what the text states on this page, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this text confirm that the military power of the new Croatian state was formed within the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the police in the described manner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, under A, does Mr. Tomac say that certain institutions were in this way formed parallel with the state institutions or state organs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Tomac, say that certain defence tasks and certain important tasks were implemented through the ruling party and trustworthy people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the ruling party in Croatia at the time, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Tomac here, as the vice -- as the Deputy Prime Minister, does he say that the procurement and distribution of weapons and ammunition was carried out through the HDZ as well as the organising of production for special purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that -- yes, that's what it states here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We will still stay on page 85. This is still page 3 of the English translation -- actually, now it's page 4 of the English translation, excuse me. In the last paragraph on page 85, Mr. Tomac states: "Since the government could not be explicitly a war government, we had to be a bit devious so the inner cabinet of the government and the ministers of the most important ministries were declared as the Crisis Staff of the republic. In that way, the government really did take over the functions which a wartime government has, but it did that under the name of Crisis Staff." At the end of this paragraph on page 85, Mr. Tomac says: "Supreme staff was formed comprising soldiers, professionals, while the Crisis Staff or, rather, the government and the executive councils, as the legal and legitimate organs of the state, took over all the logistics and other assignments which a state must carry out during war so that the army could function." Is that what it states here on page 85, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was a Crisis Staff at the republic level in Croatia as well as other Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 86 on the monitor. In the B/C/S it's marked 1D00-0183, and it's on page 4 of the English translation. On page 86, Mr. Babic, Mr. Tomac explains -- Mr. Tomac is the Deputy Prime Minister of the Croatian government: "As part of that concept, we knew that it was of crucial importance for our defence to engage Croat soldiers and officers from the Yugoslav People's Army, as well as to find a means of having them cross over to our side. In this way, three objectives were being met."

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't think that that's the text that I'm seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I think we see the text now. Can you see it now, Mr. Babic? It's chapter 2, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, let us know if the text doesn't appear on time so that we could intervene. So Mr. Tomac says: "That is how three objectives were achieved. First, we got professional officers, which we were short of. Second, we considerably weakened and destroyed from the inside the Yugoslav People's Army. Third, we created the possibility for numerous paramilitary armed formations of patriots throughout Croatia link up into a united or unified Croatian army under the single -- under single command. Much wisdom, tact, negotiations, secret meetings were needed to get 17.000 officers to cross over to our side." At the end of this paragraph, Mr. Tomac says: "The arrival of numerous generals, admirals, colonels and other officers to our ranks was a decisive turn in the war, because they knew all the failings of the JNA as well as their plans, and were able to prepare the best response to the aggression." Does that appear on page 86, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that many Croatian officers, en masse, crossed to the side of the new Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I knew about that. I don't know exactly how many of them did that. Also, the Serbian side tried to bring Serb cadres over. I've already talked about what I knew about this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at page 87 in the B/C/S on the monitor now, where Mr. Tomac explains how the officers crossed to their side. Page 87 is marked 1D00-0184. In the English, it's at the bottom of page 4. Mr. Tomac, on page 87, states: "In the implementation of the mentioned strategy, we acted on several levels and used different methods. We made timely decisions whereby all the status rights were guaranteed to the officers of the so-called JNA, who crossed to our side (ranks, salaries, apartments.) We exerted pressure through well-done propaganda. We did not just inform about these appeals. Through certain secret channels and people who worked on important people from the so-called JNA, we acted both individually and ex-institutionally. All in all, we managed to win over to our side very quickly practically all of the Croats. With that, our army grew considerably stronger and the so-called JNA was destroyed from the inside." Is that what it states here, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at page 91 on the screen, which is marked 1D00-0188. This is a text that is at the bottom, actually, of page 4 in English, and the top of page 5 of the English translation. On page 91, in the middle of the page, just below -- under paragraph 1, begins the text that I'm about to read to you now, Mr. Babic, and it states as follows: "The turnaround in the war occurred precisely at the moment when we began to deal with the Yugoslav People's Army on the entire territory of Croatia like the enemy with whom we were waging war and when we began to behave in relation to it in that way on our entire territory." And now we continue on page 5 in the English translation: "This beginning of the turnaround also occurred in Slavonski Brod when trains which were transporting weapons from Slovenia were very successfully attacked and when we acquired the first tanks, mortars, and the first anti-aircraft and anti-tank weapons. Still, the turnaround was in the decision to block the barracks and, in preparation of attacks against those barracks and weapons, warehouses which we felt could provide a turnaround in the war, if we managed to seize them. Capturing the barracks gave new impetus to us and changed the ratio of forces in weaponry in our favour. This also helped in the army's decision to withdraw from Croatia. The decision to block barracks on the entire territory of Croatia was reached at a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Republic of Croatia at the proposal of President Greguric, with the prior agreement of President Tudjman." Is this what it states on page 91, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the attack on the trains transporting weapons to Slavonia, is that what you were talking about during your testimony, Mr. Babic? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did we also mention taking over barracks, large barracks in Slavonia in September?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now may we have page 102 of the B/C/S placed on the monitor. And it is 1D00-198, which is the top of page 5 of the English version. May we scroll down, please. Down the page. Now, on page 102, Mr. Tomac says the following: "When already from the 23rd to the 26th of September I found myself in Rome at a meeting of the federal council of the Transnational Radical Party, at which there were representatives from the parliaments of 40 countries, and where for the first time abroad a resolution was brought completely to the advantage of Croatia, I endeavoured to find an opportune moment and have talks in the Vatican as well, because I thought that the Vatican diplomacy was one of the most important in the world." Is that what it says on page 102, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on the next page, 103, and the B/C/S is 1D00-0199, and it's also on page 5 of the English translation, and it says the following in the middle of the paragraph -- it's a long paragraph: "Archbishop Touran and his associates received us very warmly. I asked the support of the Vatican in our definite decision that on the 7th of October we should not extend the moratorium on the application of the declaration of independence and sovereignty of Croatia as an independent state." Is that what it says in the text, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May we now have page 104 displayed, please. And we are still on page 5 of the English. At the very top, it says the following: "What I was promised I was very satisfied with. It was stated that the Vatican was doing everything through its secret diplomacy, both in the east and the west, to stop the war and that a number of states would recognise Slovenia and Croatia simultaneously, and the other republics which so desire. It was even promised, which later came to pass, that the Vatican, both as a state, would make a precedent and would be among the first group of countries to recognise Slovenia and Croatia." Is that what it says on that page?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Vatican was indeed amongst the first countries to recognise Croatia's independence in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Vatican, by recognising on the 13th of January 1992 these states was the first country, the first state, to recognise Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first state was in fact Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Now may we have page 110 displayed on the monitor. It is 1D00-0206 of the B/C/S. And in English, it is at the bottom of page 5 and the top of page 6. On page 110, in the middle, Mr. Tomac says as follows: "At a closed session with the presidents of the Crisis Staffs, we analysed in detail how to implement the blockade of the barracks. We decided how we were going to, in our joint actions, de-structure the ranks of the JNA. I demanded that the question of responsibility be decided once and for all of all those who remained in the JNA. Now, when Croatia is formally being constituted as an independent state, anybody who remains in the occupying army, although does not personally take part in military operations and crimes, does bear the moral and political responsibility. I also demanded that through all possible channels, every man amongst the soldiers and officers be reached who were neutral until now and who could join our side, to be told quite openly that we can no longer guarantee their safety or the safety of their families if they stay on the side of the occupier, and that they will be treated as enemies regardless of their personal conduct." And at the end of that paragraph, Mr. Tomac said: "This certainly didn't refer to those who, in agreement with us, remained in the barracks and in their places so that should a conflict break out and the need to take over the barracks, that they could work from inside." Is that what it says on page 110, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know about the blockade of the barracks in Sibenik in 1991, the second half of 1991, that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the commander of the barracks, I think his name was Lakic, a lieutenant colonel of the JNA, that his wife was brought in front of the barracks and she was told to call her husband, Commander Lakic, to hand over the barracks, and she shouted out to him, "Don't surrender, because these people are Ustashas," and then she was killed before his very eyes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about that event but I don't know the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Lieutenant Colonel Lakic's wife was an ethnic Croat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May we have page 114 displayed on the monitor now, please. And that is document 1D00-0210, which is page 6 of the English. On page 114, Mr. Tomac writes about how the consul of the United States of America -- or rather that he explained to him the fact that we did not attack some barracks and come by weapons and ammunition, had we not come by that, everything would have been over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, is what you say also in the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a moment for me to check that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would seem that I have made a mistake, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the page numbers. The sentence I just read out is to be found -- well, it would appear that it is 114 but in fact it's page 115 that that is on, where it says: "I explained to him the fact that had we not come by ammunition in some of the barracks, everything would have been over." So it's actually page 115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... go to 114, you'll get to 115 when the time comes. Go to 114, which is where you referred us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, at the bottom of page 114, in the B/C/S version, is that what it says, in the penultimate line? Is this what it says: "I explained the fact that to him that had we not attacked certain barracks and come by arms and ammunition, everything would already have been finished, over"? Thank you, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have that on our screen, Mr. Milovancevic, at page 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the English translation, underneath page 114, where Greguric, the Prime Minister, is mentioned, you have page 115, and by mistake, this text has been attached to page 115, whereas it is in fact at the bottom of page 114. There has been a mix-up there. I don't know whether you're able to see that. But if we continued along the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see that, Mr. Milovancevic, but then you should have said that, that we should -- we should disregard page 115 and what is said there as page 115 is part of 114. We have only one sentence under page 114. That's all we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. It's precisely as you've just described it but I didn't notice that until you drew my attention to it. I wasn't aware of this misunderstanding but I have realised that that is so once you have pointed it out to me. So please bear with me. I would have done that beforehand had I noticed the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will bear with you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this would be a good time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be. It will give you the time also to sort out your exhibit. Thank you very much. Court adjourned. We'll come back at quarter to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just briefly for witness planning purposes, I'm wondering -- and I told Defence counsel that I would raise this point. I'm wondering if for witness planning purposes we could get an indication from Defence counsel if they still plan to finish their cross-examination of the witness no later than Tuesday, as they had earlier indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, are you able to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have planned to finish our cross-examination of this witness on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see on the screen page 220 of Mr. Tomac's book. The marking is 1D00-0297, and this text is on page 7 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we start reading the text, Mr. Babic, you have mentioned the Rijeka Corps of the JNA. Do you know that General Cad was the commander of the Rijeka Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 220, it reads -- actually, the text speaks about the Rijeka negotiators and it follows the course of the negotiations. It says here: "Three to five times a day and during the night for over two months, they were trying to persuade General Cad and his associates. In cooperation with the psychiatric service of the main medical staff, a psychological and psychiatric profile was made of the commander of the 13th Corps. We also got hold of General Cad's son and included him, and many other family members and friends of the key men of the 13th Corps who constantly exerted pressure." Can you see this text on page 220, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This pressure on JNA officers, was it exerted by the new Croatian authorities in the course of 1991 in order for them to surrender JNA units to the Croatian authorities? Is that something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you any details of that. I can just tell you something in very general terms along the lines of what I have already told you about the blockade of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now have page 229 of the book on the screen. The marking is 1D00-0306. The translation is on page 8. On page 229 in the first paragraph, on the top, the penultimate sentence, Mr. Tomac, the Vice-Prime Minister of the Croatian government, says: "During the three-month siege of Vukovar, all members of the government were at their disposal at any time, day or night. The men in Vukovar could call us any night, even at 3.00 in the morning, if necessary. Most telephone calls were made by Marin Vidic, Bili, and Dr. Bosanac." The next paragraph on page 229 says the following. "In the government we tried to visit the places where the situation was the worst. Because of that, and because of the fact that I was in charge of a large part of Slavonia in the Crisis Staff, and since the situation there was the most difficult, it was only logical that I was the one who went to Slavonski Brod and Slavonia most often." At the end of that paragraph, there is a sentence which reads: "The battle for Slavonia was the most decisive battle in the fight for Croatia. Our enemy suffered a decisive defeat in Slavonia. There were several decisive battles in that struggle. During the three-month siege of Vukovar, the sole force of the elite JNA units was crushed and the planned offensive was stopped, and the goal of the offensive was to conquer whole Slavonia." Is this what it reads on this page, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there was a long battle being conducted in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 417 on the screen. And that is the last page from the book that we are going to put to the witness. And the marking is 1D00-0392, and this is the last passage on page 8 of the translation. On page 417, at the very top of it, Mr. Tomac, Vice-Prime Minister of the Croatian government, says: "I again remember the planned coup d'etat on 25th January 1991, the film about Spegelj, and everything that had happened at the time which merits a separate chapter. Greguric and Spegelj had a very strong bond and a very friendly connection. They were the main people who obtained the first weapons at a time when it meant risking their lives." Do you see this text on page 417, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this text, Mr. Tomac mentions Mr. Greguric and Mr. Spegelj. Can you please tell us, who was Mr. Greguric and who was Mr. Spegelj at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January 1991, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And before that, and after that. In general terms, if you can just briefly tell us who they are.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spegelj was the minister of defence in the government of Croatia at the time. And Greguric, I don't know what he did in January, but he was Prime Minister as of the autumn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Greguric was the Prime Minister of the Croatian government, the government of democratic unity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this book, Mr. Tomac speaks about the government of Croatia, which tricked everybody by changing the name of the government into the Crisis Staff and thus playing with the Brioni moratorium; isn't that the fact, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the passages that you read out from the book, then I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether I have moved for this book to be introduced as a Defence exhibit. If I haven't, I would like to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to make two points about this exhibit. First, I would forecast that we will argue that it has extremely limited value. Obviously this person has not come and testified. Basically what the Defence counsel has done has -- is read -- brought this -- the portions of the book and elicited very little comment from the witness who is actually here, so the part that -- to the extent that there is material here that's beyond what the witness has commented on, I would -- I'm just going to argue that it has very little value. This witness has not come here to testify or be cross-examined. The second point, Your Honour, is that these are very limited excerpts from a 589-page book. We have not had an opportunity, obviously, to review the entire book. We will endeavour to do so and it may come -- it may be that we will seek the admission of larger portions in order to give context and completeness to the very limited sentences that are excerpted. There are several sentences from each page, and so I just forecast that we may do that. Given those qualifications, I have no objection to it being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, that's your right, at the end of the trial, when you argue, to argue the relevance of the document. It is your right when you re-examine, or at any other stage, to seek the greater part of the book and put it into evidence if you so wish. Mr. Milovancevic, the Chamber wants to repeat what it said to you yesterday. The Chamber said to you yesterday, what is the point of reading through a whole document, getting it on the transcript, and then asking for it to be admitted as an exhibit? Why must it be read twice over? We are burdening the record unnecessarily. What is it that this exhibit is going to tell us which you have not already read?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appreciate your words, and I believe that you're right. As Defence counsel, I can move for the admission of those pages that have been presented to the witness before the Trial Chamber. I used the principle of work that the Trial Chamber adopted when it came to the book written by General Kadijevic, and I thought it would be necessary to admit into evidence the entire book in order to be -- to enable the Prosecution to use the entire text, but if you believe that only the excerpts that we have read out should be admitted, I am prepared to move for that. I didn't want to complicate our lives any further, and I thought that my proposal for admission would be the simplest thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I appreciate what you say. I don't entirely agree with you. It was made quite clear yesterday that there is no purpose whatsoever in reading a whole document and then asking for the document to be admitted into evidence. It may very well be that there is a case for admitting it into evidence this time because there are parts that you have not read and it is important that the Prosecution gets an opportunity to read the entire document. But that said, and bearing in mind the comment from the Chamber yesterday, the Chamber does not understand why you still did today what you were warned against yesterday. All you could have done is you could have shown the witness this document, and asked that it be tendered into evidence, then ask him the question, the one or two questions that you asked him to comment about the contents and just refer to those parts. You haven't asked this witness extensively about this -- about the passages that you read. All you asked him to do is, Do you agree that that's what's written? And he says yes because that's what he reads there. We all see that that's what's written. We spent the whole of this last session going through this document and this is valuable time that we could have used doing other things. I want to suggest to you that please try to focus on the case. This document doesn't say anything about the period of the indictment. So it is very difficult -- the last point here, the very last point, talks about the 25th of January 1991, which is outside the period of the indictment. It does not help us just to read through the document and then ask at the end that it be admitted into evidence. You could admit it and you could have asked the witness to comment on those one or two points that you asked him to comment on. I hope that this does not recur. The document is admitted in its entirety into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I would like to provide you with an explanation. I propose for this exhibit to be admitted and I have not finished the examination of the witness about the circumstances that are described in the book. That may be my mistake. That's one part of the explanation. The second part of the explanation is that I asked for the admission of the entire document as a matter of principle, to avoid any objections on the part of the Prosecution that we are using only excerpts. In any case, I will adhere to the instructions that you have provided me with, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. The document in its entirety has already been admitted into evidence. It is now an exhibit. And if the Court -- the Chamber has asked you to proceed, and by saying "Proceed," you are most welcome to ask this witness any further questions from the document, if you want to do so. That explanation really doesn't explain anything. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in this book, the Deputy Prime Minister of Croatia writes about the activities of the Croatian government. The first Croatian government of democratic unity in the period from the 4th of August 1991 onwards. I put several questions to you regarding the relationship of the new Croatian authorities, or the attitude of the new Croatian authorities towards the JNA. Do you know that a large number of Croatian officers left the JNA even though they were under oath and they crossed over to the side of the new Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These officers, just like all the other officers of any ethnicity, took an oath in the JNA that they would preserve the territorial integrity and the sovereignty of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I assume that they did. That was the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I was specific enough. Did the officers, when they took their duties, when they entered the military academy, did they take such an oath?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, just like any soldier would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The mentioned Croatian officers who crossed to the Croatian side in the process of secession, were they released from that oath that they gave to the JNA before they crossed over to the other side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me about details. I don't know any details about this. I heard many stories about that but I cannot really say right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Do you have information that in a certain number of barracks, there were activities from the inside by officers - for example, ethnic Croatians and Slovenians - that they betrayed their colleagues in the barracks and that they were working for the other side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Deputy Prime Minister of the Croatian government, Mr. Tomac, say in this book that the new Croatian authorities asked all the Croatian officers to leave the JNA except for those that it left so that they could work on the inside for the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read that book. I don't know anything about it other than what you cited here, so I can just repeat what you read out here and what I saw on screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Croatian armed forces used weapons which they confiscated in the attacked and seized barracks and weapons depots in the course of 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they did. Why would they take them otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You, as the president of the Krajina government, did you feel the effects of those weapons in the territory of Krajina? Were you under fire in that period? Are you aware of the armed conflicts with the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about the armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Croatian leadership first adopted the decision to blockade the barracks and after that decided that the barracks should be attacked. Do you know about that and do you know if the JNA barracks were attacked in the first half of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the barracks were attacked, but I told you what I knew about the three stages of the barracks blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that because conflicts broke out in the autumn of 1991, several attempts were made to achieve a cease-fire and that there were a total of 14 cease-fires which the JNA, as the regular armed force, concluded with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in Geneva on the 23rd of November 1991, headed by Special UN Envoy Mr. Vance, an agreement was reached on a cease-fire on the 23rd of November 1991? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was this agreement signed by the president of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman; the president of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic; federal secretary for national defence, General Kadijevic, who also participated in the negotiations under the mediation of Mr. Vance? This is the agreement that we are talking about, isn't it, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the purpose -- or let me rephrase the question, excuse me, Mr. Babic. Are you aware whether these cease-fire agreements provided the possibility that the encircled JNA units pull out with their equipment and personnel from these besieged barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the final cease-fire agreements on the pullout of the JNA units from Croatia, which was supposed to take place within the whole framework of the implementation of the Vance-Owen plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in September, October, November and December, very serious fighting was waged between JNA units and Croatian armed forces comprised by the ZNG and the Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we now please show on the monitor Prosecution document from the 65 ter list number 1227. This document in front of you states, in the upper left-hand corner, Military District Command, it was dated the 19th of September 1991, and underneath that, it says: "A directive excerpt of the commander of the 1st Military District for the operation in Slavonia." Is that what it states here, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under section 1, paramilitary formations of Croatia -- well, perhaps we should look at the document -- the end of the document first to see who signed the document. Could we show the last page of the document on the monitor; it's marked 007692383. In the lower right-hand corner, you can see the name of the commander. Could you please read the name of the commander who drafted this directive.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states here, Commander Colonel General Nikola Uzelac. Actually, somebody signed it on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Next to this signature, is there a stamp there as well as an indication that somebody had signed this document for him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go back to page 1 of this directive now, please. On page 1, before it appears on the monitor, Mr. Babic, under section 1, or paragraph 1, headed, "Paramilitary formations of Croatia," it states: "In the zone of the 1st Military District, it is estimated that the paramilitary formations of the Republic of Croatia number between 45 to 50.000 armed people -- men, of which 28 to 32.000 are located in Eastern Slavonia. The main forces are grouped in Osijek, Vukovar, and Vinkovci, a settlement in the immediate vicinity of these towns and around the roads there as well as in the area of Western Slavonia broader sector of Okucani, Pakrac, Slavonski Brod." It further states that: "The forces in Eastern Slavonia are deployed as follows: "A: ZNG numbering from 12.000 to 14.000, in brigades Vukovar, Osijek, Vinkovci and probably Djakovo. "B: MUP forces numbering from 10 to 11.000, grouped in three police units, Osijek, Vukovar, Vinkovci, with about 12 police stations. And then the Vinkovci forces in the local communes there. In Western Slavonia --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down and could we have the text in B/C/S on the screen. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you hear that? You're being asked to slow down, Mr. Milovancevic, because you're moving too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to pay attention to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only see up to paragraph B on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now scroll this first page on the monitor. This is fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, can you see the whole page now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I wonder if, before we read this entire document, maybe we could have some foundational questions about whether the witness knows anything about this, because this is outside the area that he was responsible for at that time period. This is Slavonia and he was responsible for the Krajina. So I wonder if, before we get too far afield on this, whether maybe we could find out if the witness will even be able to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am showing the witness this document in order to put questions to him relating to specific facts. In 1991, the witness was the president of the SAO Krajina government, defence minister, commander of the Territorial Defence, and claiming that he had no idea what was going on in a part of the Krajina territory for me is not acceptable because it cannot be right. The witness will respond whether he knows anything about this or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The issue that is being raised is for you just to lay a foundation for the document, and find out from the witness whether he does know anything about the document for the simple reason that this document deals with an area which was outside his area of jurisdiction at the time. And laying that kind of foundation is a simple thing. You can ask two, three, perhaps at most five questions to lay that kind of foundation. You don't need to go too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, are you familiar with General Nikola Uzelac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two generals with that last name. One of them was the commander of the Banja Luka Corps and one was commander of the Zagreb Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the fact that the 5th Banja Luka Corps was carrying out operations in Western Slavonia under the command of General Uzelac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And these operations, did they encompass the places that are mentioned in this directive; Okucani, Pakrac, and the Novska sector?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely, but it was that general area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. You said that Croatia, during the secession period, was creating its armed forces within the framework of the police; is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that as far as I can recall, the National Guards Corps was formed within the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether the National Guards Corps, the ZNG, in 1991, acted with -- within brigade formations? Did you hear if the ZNG had brigades as part of its composition?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the Osijek, Vukovar and Vinkovci police administrations? Did you hear that they existed as such?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they did exist because these are major centres and there were police administrations, so-called police administrations in major administrative centres, and these were major centres so I assume they existed in these towns, but I don't know that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the arming of the Croatian Democratic Community, the ruling party in Croatia, in the spring and -- in the summer and autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what appeared in the Serbian media and what was shown in the footage shown in January 1991. From there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Earlier, I showed you excerpts from the book of the Deputy Prime Minister of the Croatian government, Dr. Zdravko Tomac, stating that in the conditions of the Brioni moratorium, and the obligation of Croatia to respect the moratorium, arming was carried out within the party framework. Does that correspond to the information that you have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if, in -- if there were conflicts between the Croatian newly established forces and the regular JNA forces in that area in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these were quite heavy combat operations and conflicts and that there were victims or casualties on both sides?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in those armed conflicts, it was the Serb settlements inhabited by Serbs that suffered throughout Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in October, November and December, 1991, tens of thousands of refugees from Slavonia sought refuge by crossing into Bosnia, going into Banja Luka and other places in the face of the Croatian army onslaught?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a fax sent by the Yugoslav government to the United Nations about the fact that in those operations in Western Slavonia by the Croatian army, that many Serbian villages were destroyed, houses destroyed, and the population expelled?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the document but I do remember the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear complaints made by the JNA to the effect that the Croatian armed formations used every truce and cease-fire to reorganise themselves, to recoup and attack the JNA again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where and when?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the period from the beginning of September 1991 to the end of 1991, during which time as many as 14 truces were agreed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in the Krajina area, the SAO Krajina, the JNA was mostly on the offensive. In Western Slavonia, sometime from November and December, the JNA was withdrawing. So that was the balance of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about a memorandum of an agreement concluded between the JNA and the Croatian armed forces with the mediation of the European Community in the person of Ambassador Dirk Jan van Houten? I think that was his name, unless I'm mistaken. That was the 8th of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May we display on the monitor now, please, a document -- I don't know whether it's already been tendered. Is it already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I go ahead, I'd like to tender the previous document, the directive dated September that we discussed earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you were still laying a foundation for it, because you picked up an objection while you were asking questions on this document that's on the screen right now. Are you done with it? Thank you very much. Well, the document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what the basis is for admitting this document into evidence. There has been no discussion about the document except that the -- except the identification of the person who signed the document. But as far as the contents of the document, unless I missed something, I don't think there was any discussion about the contents -- the actual contents of the document, any verification by the witness of the contents, or the circumstances, or anything in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Whiting, I think the Chamber has just decided to go along with the guidelines that it gave on admission of documents at the beginning. It will look at the probative value of the document at the time of assessing the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, you wanted to put a document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I was going to ask that document -- Prosecution document from the 65 ter list number 2 be put on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Babic, a memorandum of the agreement signed in Zagreb on the 8th of October 1991 by General Andrija Raseta, president of the Secretariat for National Defence, and Stjepan Adamic, deputy defence minister of Croatia, and Colonel Imre Agotic, member of the Supreme Staff of the Croatian army under the auspices of the European Community. Might this document be shown on the screens. In order to make the best use of our time, Mr. Babic -- ah, the document has appeared on our screens. It's a memorandum of the agreement. And could the second page of this two-page document be shown on the screens. Page 2, please. On page 2, Mr. Babic, it says the following: "That the document was compiled in Zagreb on the 8th of October 1991, the signatories, with their signatures, General Andrija Raseta, Stjepan Adamic, Colonel Imre Agotic, and Ambassador Dirk Jan van Houten. Is that so, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can read that there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, may we go back to page 1 of the document on the monitor, please. In point 1, note is taken of the following, that the parties mentioned agreed in the presence of the auspices of the European Community, that they agreed on the following: That a general cease-fire come into force on the territory of Croatia on the 18th of October -- on the 8th of October 1991 at 1800 hours which will be strictly respected by both sides while taking part at the Peace Conference on Yugoslavia. Point 3 says the following: "That the blockades on land and sea imposed by both sides with all their forces along the Adriatic coast and in the hinterland, will be simultaneously disbanded, dismantled with the aim of enabling the free passage of people, foodstuffs and various other goods." The last sentence in this paragraph, point 3, states the following: "The JNA units can leave with their means of transport, technical materiel, untouched weapons, military equipment and other movable military property. " And then point 4 says that: "The blockade of the barracks in Borogaj [phoen], in Zagreb, will be disbanded immediately and that the withdrawal of the troops stationed there would begin immediately and end by 1800 hours on Saturday, the 12th of October 1991." Have you heard about this document? Do you know it, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the document specifically, but as I say, there were a number of agreements on a truce and cease-fire and the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So as early on as the 8th of October 1991, the federal authorities and the JNA, as their armed force, drew up an agreement with the government of Croatia by which the surrounded units would withdraw from the territory of Croatia. Isn't that right, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was on a cease-fire, yes, and the withdrawal, yes, and the agreements were violated the whole time. So what more can I tell you about that? How else can I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that by these agreements, it was envisaged that the Croatian side would allow the JNA units under siege to pull out its men and materiel, the equipment it had in the barracks under siege?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of several specific agreements after the fighting that took place, that the Knin Corps discussed, after the Knin Corps actions in Zadar, Sibenik and Sinj, an agreement was reached between the commanders of the corps and the Croatian authorities to lift the siege so that the JNA units could be pulled out along with their equipment and materiel. So I know about those events better than I do the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether, along with great -- a great deal of problems and effort, that the agreements were implemented on the ground? Did the units in fact leave Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The withdrawal evolved in stages. It lasted for many months and went on until the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This JNA withdrawal, did it also envisage -- was it also envisaged by the so-called Vance Plan or, rather, the United Nations plan to send peace forces to Yugoslavia at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that the first foundations for the United Nations peace plan, or the Vance Plan, in Yugoslavia were laid in Geneva on the 23rd of November 1991? And that this was implemented in January, February and the months that followed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was signed by Milosevic, Tudjman, and Kadijevic through the mediation of Vance on the 23rd of November in Geneva, and the plan was adopted and accepted in the UN Secretary-General's report in February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you, as a witness, told us that the real plan of the federal government of Milosevic and the JNA, was to occupy a portion of Croatian territory. Now we see that it was much earlier, if we compare it to the Vance Plan, that the JNA was in fact withdrawing from Croatia and it was doing so under fighting but it was leaving Croatian territory. Do you see any discrepancy between that and your assertions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the JNA did withdraw from certain parts of Croatia. However, on the -- it stayed on in the Serb territories. And in territories which were supposed to remain within the new state, right up until the 12th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the population of SAO Krajina and then Republika Srpska Krajina? Was it physically and biologically jeopardised by the new Croatian authorities and its armed formations in that period? And I'm talking about 1991 and the beginning of 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is meant by "biologically jeopardised," Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was thinking of the threat of physical destruction, annihilation by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The physical you have mentioned. I'm asking about biological.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the explanation I gave should explain what I meant when I said "biological." I meant their survival. So the Serb population in Croatia was threatened with extermination and physical destruction by the Croatian authorities. That was the crux of my question but I can rephrase it so that we do away with any dilemmas, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You meant extermination. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a functionary of the SAO Krajina -- Knin, actually, Republika Srpska Krajina, and as a man who in February 1991 appealed in Geneva to all the relevant organs in the world for protection, for the protection of the lives and rights of people, do you think that the Serbs were jeopardised, were under threat, on the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said -- I've already spoken about the escalation of the conflict. Until February 1992, I said what this related to; violation of human rights, dismissal from jobs, et cetera. I also spoke about the incidents that broke out, the escalation of conflicts and violence in the beginning of the war. Now your question is a very general one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. That will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, please, may we have -- or, rather, the document that was on the screen, the memorandum of the agreement between the JNA and the Croatian side through the mediation of the European Community, may this be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 240, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now, may we display on the monitor a Prosecution document from the 65 ter list, Exhibit number 1272, please. It is a bulletin, bulletin number 110 of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, dated December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before this document appears -- ah, here we have it on our screens. Mr. Babic, do you know that the Federal Secretariat for National Defence during 1991 issued bulletins of this kind, that is to say periodical reports to inform the public and, of course, the officer cadre of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read them. I do know that bulletins of this kind were published, or announcements. Whether they were called bulletins or whatever, I don't know. Probably they were, probably they were referred to as bulletins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May we have page 1 of the document displayed, the bulletin number 110. There are several pages to that document but I'd like to have the page 1 displayed. And on this first page, Mr. Babic, you can see that it says the number of the bulletin, which is 110, that it was published in Belgrade on 3rd of December 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I wonder if Defence counsel has a translation of the document in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have an English translation, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a slight problem. I didn't know that the document was not translated, although it is a 65 ter exhibit. I believe that there was a translation. This may be my mistake. Can it be marked for identification and we will subsequently deliver its translation, if the Trial Chamber thinks that this might be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we decide on that, Mr. Whiting, apparently this is a Prosecution document. You can enlighten us on whether there is an English translation of the document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we don't have -- we don't seem to have an English one in the e-court system. I've asked our case manager to search the broader system to see if a translation has been done of the document. Perhaps this could be put aside until Monday to see if we have a translation. It's going to be awkward to try to use this document in court without a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you agreeable to that, Mr. Milovancevic? To delay dealing with this document until there is an English translation? Are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe that everybody will be better off; the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution, and also we will be better off if we have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Then the B/C/S document will be marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification number 241, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, which would have appeared on the screen in English, a violation of peace -- cease-fire is described. Do you know any detail about whether after the Geneva agreement on the 23rd November 1991, there was indeed a cease-fire or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, maybe we didn't understand each other. I asked you, and I thought you agreed, whether you would be prepared to defer dealing with this document until we have the English translation. And I thought you said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I am going to do exactly that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I just -- I was surprised you were still dealing with it now. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you've told us that you know that on the 23rd November 1991, an agreement was signed laying the foundation of the so-called Vance Plan. This was a cease-fire agreement and laying a foundation for the peacekeeping operation of the United Nations in Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if that cease-fire agreement that was signed in Geneva on the 23rd November 1991, was it honoured? Was it implemented? Or did the fierce fighting continue even after that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. I know that both sides accused each other of cease-fire violations. I believe that the fighting in Western Slavonia lasted longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Do you know if, in addition to the fighting in Western Slavonia, in the second half of 1991, in October, and especially after the 23rd of November 1991, there was fighting elsewhere, in other regions of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that. There was fighting from Vukovar down to Dubrovnik, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what happened to the 9th Knin Corps at the time? Was that corps engaged in an operation of some sort, deblocking the barracks? Were there any fights?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Knin Corps was engaged in several operations for deblocking the barracks. This was in Sinj, in Sibenik, in Zadar, and also there was something in Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you have also mentioned the armed conflict that took place in the village called Kijevo. This happened on the 25th and 26th of August 1991; is that correct, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were armed Croatian units in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a police station there of the Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, how many armed men did this police station have on its strength?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many Croatian policemen were arrested by the JNA during that operation on the 26th of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that there were 52 prisoners in Kijevo, or 62, would that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know anything about that, or I don't remember. It wouldn't mean anything. I can believe you if you say that that was the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about an armed conflict in Kijevo? Was there one or wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the European Community; i.e., Lord Carrington, intervened with the Yugoslav authorities about the fighting in Kijevo on account of the destruction of religious buildings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the church in the village of Kijevo was indeed damaged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who inflicted that damage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I've heard, the church was shelled from tanks, at the beginning of the attack on Kijevo, and later on it was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say as far as you've heard. When did you hear, who did you hear it from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from some people who were members of the JNA. They told me that at the beginning of the attack on Kijevo, there was tank fire opened on the church in Kijevo and every hit, every hit was applauded and later on I heard that it was destroyed, the church. I don't know how many days later I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in the Kijevo church, there were armed members of Croatian units and whether they opened fire from the church tower?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a film was made, a TV film was made, about the situation in Kijevo, after the armed conflict, and this film features the church and the surrounding houses that were damaged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember one clip from Kijevo and I've already spoken about that here. I saw it on Belgrade TV, and there was something about the flag being taken down by Martic, and some statements by the reservists. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Can we have on the monitor 65 ter Exhibit number 245. And before we actually see the document, on the document let me tell you, Mr. Babic, that this is a letter issued by the SAO Krajina SUP from Knin to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the federal Presidency, and the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia in Zagreb. You can see this letter on the screen now. Can we scroll down in order to see the entire text on the monitor. As far as I can tell, this is not the document that I looked for. Let me see if I gave you the right number. I asked for the document number 244. This is a different document. Mr. Babic, my question was not relative to the document you can see in front of you at the moment. And before we resolve the -- this issue, can you please tell us, Mr. Babic, whether you heard of the letter that the -- that Milan Martic sent on the 3rd of March 1995, to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the federal SUP, and the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia relative to the situation in Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This document has already been admitted into evidence. In this document, Mr. Babic, as the secretary of the SUP, did he inform the Presidency in Belgrade, the federal SUP and the MUP in Zagreb, that there were blockades in Kijevo, that the locals were blocking the passage through the village, they were preventing people from exercising their official tasks and that the SUP got in touch with the police administration in Sibenik in view of some negotiations about Kijevo? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember these events, and I've already told you that. And I've also told you that there were barricades around Kijevo for a long time. Those had been put up by the Serbs from local -- from surrounding villages and at one point the villagers of Kijevo responded in a similar way, and this was my comment to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Martic, as the secretary of the Knin SUP, sent a similar letter again on the 25th of April 1991, and he pointed to the problem of Kijevo and he said that the locals of Kijevo are being -- were being used as the scapegoats by the Croatian police? In that letter, he offered the delegation of Kijevo a political solution to all the problems. Are you aware of that letter? That letter was presented to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Babic, that the barricades erected by the locals was one problem and that a second problem was the existence of the Croatian police station which numbered a lot of armed members of the Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether this is a good time to end for today. It is 7.00. I believe that the moment is good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is indeed a good time, Mr. Milovancevic. The matter will stand adjourned to Monday, the 6th of March, at 9.00 in the morning, in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
